name: Postal Museum
intro: The Postal Museum, or Postamúzeum, occupies the Benczúr House at Benczúr utca 27 in Terézváros, a late nineteenth-century mansion that later became a cultural centre for postal workers. Its permanent exhibition follows Hungarian postal, telegraph and telephone history through vehicles, switchboards, a period post office and hands-on machines.
about: The Postamúzeum is Hungary’s postal museum, housed in the Benczúr-ház at Benczúr utca 27, in the sixth district. The museum describes itself as a specialist museum with a national collecting remit, and it has been based in this house since 2012.

The permanent exhibition, titled “Elsők között…” (“Among the first…”), fills five rooms on the second floor and follows the innovations of the Hungarian Royal Post, from the first Hungarian postcard of 1869 to the Lakihegy radio tower of 1933. Headline objects include a Hughes printing telegraph of 1867, a motor tricycle of 1900, a liaison car of 1906, a manual telephone exchange of 1929 and a 1930s post-office room with a working pneumatic tube.

Much of the display is meant to be handled: the museum lists manual switchboards, Morse and telex machines, a touchscreen games station, letter-bundle making and a demonstration of sealing a valuables sack. A temporary exhibition changes roughly every six months, and earlier shows are moved into the archive section of the museum’s website, which also offers an online 3D walkthrough.

The house stands in Terézváros, the district around Andrássy út, and the link is historic: the museum opened in the Saxlehner Palace on Andrássy út in 1972 and stayed there until it moved to Benczúr utca in 2012. It is a specialist stop that suits visitors, and families in particular, who enjoy working machines.
tips: Check the museum’s official page before you go for current visiting arrangements, ticket categories and guided tours; the site has an English version, but its pages are written first in Hungarian.
The hands-on stations, including a Morse key and manual switchboards, make this a good choice for families. The museum also lists museum-education programmes for school groups.
The online MúzeumDigitár, photo archive and virtual walkthrough on the official site are useful for deciding what to look for before you arrive.
Andrássy út is the natural walk from here, and the former Saxlehner Palace, the museum’s home from 1972, is on it. Ask staff about photography rules when you arrive.

history.intro: The museum’s collection is older than its home. The two stories, one of an institution, one of a house, meet only in 2012.

sections.heading: From a telegraph room to a national museum
paragraphs: The collection began modestly in 1881, when spare telegraph apparatus was gathered in a first-floor room of Budapest’s main post office. In 1890 the minister Gábor Baross ordered a combined post and telegraph museum, which the museum treats as its founding. A post, telegraph and telephone hall at the 1896 Millennium Exhibition was meant to become the core of an independent museum, but it was later demolished, and from 1899 to 1945 part of the collection was shown at the Transport Museum.
A reorganised Postamúzeum opened in 1955 in the Postal Directorate General building as a specialist museum with national scope. It opened in the Saxlehner Palace on Andrássy út in 1972.

sections.heading: The Egyedi Palace on Benczúr utca
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia says the house was built in the late nineteenth century, then at Nagy János utca 27, as a residence and office building for Lajos Egyedi, whose family wealth came from a spirits distillery in Újpest. It names the architect as Oszkár Marmorek and mentions stained-glass windows by Miksa Róth; the article gives no exact year of construction.
Hungarian Wikipedia says the Hungarian Royal Postal Charity Fund bought the palace in 1930, while the museum’s page dates its use as a building for the culture of postal workers from 1931.

sections.heading: The Benczúr House and the museum
paragraphs: After the early 1990s the house belonged to a postal and telecommunications cultural foundation. Hungarian Wikipedia reports that its founders decided to close it in 2009, that Magyar Posta became the sole owner in 2010, and that the Postamúzeum has received visitors on the second and third floors since 9 October 2012. The official page dates the opening of the permanent exhibition to the same day. The building is a listed monument.

name: Kolibri Theatre
intro: The Kolibri Színház, or Kolibri Children’s and Youth Theatre, stands on Jókai tér in Terézváros, close to Oktogon. Founded in 1992, it stages puppet, family and youth productions for audiences from babies to teenagers, and it also plays in two smaller venues on Andrássy út.
about: The Kolibri Gyermek- és Ifjúsági Színház is a repertory company for audiences from infancy to young adulthood. A 2016 profile on the website of the international children’s theatre association ASSITEJ described it as the only professional children’s and youth theatre in Hungary with its own company, and its official site sorts the programme into infant, child and youth categories.

It works in three venues. The main house at Jókai tér 10 presents family and fairy-tale plays and youth theatre, Kolibri Fészek at Andrássy út 74 stages performances for children aged up to nine, and Kolibri Pince at Andrássy út 77 is devoted to youth theatre. Its repertoire mixes puppet shows, family plays and youth drama; the official programme shows what is on.

The site has an English section for international bookings. It describes some of the company’s productions as non-verbal and one youth production as English-subtitled, but it does not say which of them are playing in Budapest on a given date, so check the programme and the stated age group for each show.

Jókai tér is known as the square of Hungarian literature. It was renovated in 2022, and short quotations from József Attila, Pilinszky János, Ady Endre and Kassák Lajos are displayed in the park. Across the way, on Liszt Ferenc tér, stand the Menza restaurant and the Írók Boltja bookshop, so the theatre sits among cafés and bookshops.
tips: Check the official programme for the performance, the age recommendation and the venue: the three stages are at different addresses, two of them on Andrássy út.
The programme pages are in Hungarian. If you are visiting with children who do not speak it, check the English section for non-verbal productions and ask the theatre before booking.
Tickets are sold online through the system linked from the official page. Leave time to walk through Jókai tér and its literary quotations before or after a show.
Liszt Ferenc tér is across the square, and Oktogon and Andrássy út are a short walk away. Keep phones silent during the performance and follow the staff’s guidance on photography.

history.intro: The theatre dates from 1992, but its house had a stage life long before. Hungarian Wikipedia is the only source found for the building’s history, so treat those details as reported there.

sections.heading: A house with a theatrical past
paragraphs: Jókai tér 10 went up in 1912 as a Secession-style apartment house with a cinema, the Edison, at street level. Cabaret venues followed from 1916, and in 1927 Sándor Rott opened the Komédia, which worked as the Komédia Orfeum from 1928 to 1944.

sections.heading: From post-war stage to puppet theatre
paragraphs: After the war the stage went through several names and managers. From 1954 it was a chamber theatre of the Vidám Színpad, and after a rebuilding in 1970 it served the Állami Bábszínház, the State Puppet Theatre, which used it as its chamber stage from 1976 to 1992.

sections.heading: Kolibri since 1992
paragraphs: The Budapest Metropolitan Assembly founded the Kolibri Színház in this building in 1992, according to Hungarian Wikipedia, and the company’s own English page also dates its founding to 1992. The ASSITEJ profile credits the composer and theatre director János Novák as its founder and executive and artistic director, and Hungarian Wikipedia says he led it until 2025, when János Zalán became director.

name: Liberty Bridge
address: Between Fővám tér (Pest) and Gellért tér (Buda), Budapest IX / XI
intro: Liberty Bridge, or Szabadság híd, carries road and tram traffic between Fővám tér on the Pest bank and Gellért tér at the foot of Gellért Hill. Built for the Millennium World Exhibition and opened in 1896 as the Franz Joseph Bridge, it was blown up in 1945, rebuilt, and is still crowned by bronze turul birds.
about: The Szabadság híd is a three-span cantilever lattice iron bridge, 333.6 metres long and 20.1 metres wide, with a longest span of 170.75 metres. English Wikipedia notes that, although it is a cantilever bridge, its outline imitates a chain bridge, a look that was thought more attractive at the time. Hungarian Wikipedia says the gateways are decorated with the historic Hungarian coat of arms.

Look up at the tops of the four masts for the bronze turul birds, a falcon-like bird from Hungarian mythology. Hungarian Wikipedia describes them hovering with outstretched wings 46 metres above the zero water level. The bridge is best appreciated from the embankments on either side or from a river boat, where its whole iron structure is visible.

The Pest end is at Fővám tér, in Ferencváros, and the Buda end is at Gellért tér, at the southern foot of Gellért Hill. The 2007–2009 renovation included the decorative lighting installed in 2009, which gives the bridge a distinct look after dark.

Trams cross the bridge along with road traffic. Since the 2009 reopening it has also been closed to trams and cars at some weekends for community events, and the transport authority BKK has tested the structure with every tram type in service. Check BKK for current routes and closures before you plan a crossing on foot.
tips: Check BKK for the current tram routes and any works or event closures on the bridge; it has been shut for weekend events and for works, so a planned walk across may need a plan B.
Fővám tér on the Pest side is by the Great Market Hall, and the Buda side is by Gellért tér and the Gellért Thermal Bath, so a crossing links two sights easily.
For photographs, the embankments at either end and a boat on the river show the whole bridge; the turul birds are best seen with a longer lens.
Do not climb the structure: it is dangerous, and climbing has led to the bridge being closed.

history.intro: The bridge was one of the new Danube crossings prepared for Hungary’s millennium celebrations, and it opened in 1896. Hungarian Wikipedia gives the fullest account of its building and rebuilding.

sections.heading: A bridge for the millennium
paragraphs: A law of 1893 ordered two new Danube bridges in Budapest, one of them at Fővám tér. The plan that was built was largely the work of János Feketeházy, whose design won second prize in an international competition. Work began in 1894 on foundations sunk with pneumatic caissons, and the bridge was finished in August 1896.
Emperor Franz Joseph opened it on 4 October 1896 and hammered in the last silver rivet. It was named Ferenc József híd after him, though Fővám téri híd and Vámház téri híd were also in use.

sections.heading: Destruction and rebuilding
paragraphs: The retreating German army blew up the central section on 16 January 1945. Reconstruction began in spring 1946 to designs by Pál Sávoly, and the bridge reopened on 20 August 1946 under its present name, Szabadság híd, painted grey because paint was short. English Wikipedia lists the rebuilding year as 1945, so the sources differ; the more detailed Hungarian account is followed here.

sections.heading: Renovation and the bridge today
paragraphs: Traffic stopped on the bridge on 21 August 2007 for about 15 months. Trams returned in December 2008, cyclists on 30 May 2009 and cars the day after. BKK refers to the bridge’s 2008 renovation, and in April 2024 it ran night-time load tests with every tram type in service as part of planning for a future Újbuda–Újpest tram axis that would cross it.

sources.label: BKK: New tram on Szabadság híd, load tests (2024)

seo.title: Liberty Bridge (Szabadság híd), Budapest
seo.description: Liberty Bridge links Fővám tér and Gellért tér: the 1896 Franz Joseph Bridge, its turul birds, wartime destruction, rebuilding and 2007–2009 renovation.

name: Mikszáth Kálmán Square
intro: Mikszáth Kálmán tér is a small pedestrian square in the Palace Quarter of Józsefváros, named after the novelist Kálmán Mikszáth, who lived in the house at number 1. A statue of the writer by András Kocsis stands in one corner, and terraces make the square a popular place for eating and drinking outdoors.
about: Mikszáth Kálmán tér lies in the eighth district, in the Palace Quarter behind the Hungarian National Museum. Tall buildings surround it, and it meets three streets: Reviczky, Krúdy and Szentkirályi. We Love Budapest reports that cars were banned around the turn of the millennium, and in summer the square feels like one large garden.

The landmarks are modest. The statue of Mikszáth, made by András Kocsis, stands in a corner, and Hungarian Wikipedia dates it to 1961. A commemorative plaque to the writer is by Kallós Ede, and a relief plaque for János Irinyi, the inventor of the match, is by Horvay János. The house at number 1 is now the building of the humanities faculty of Pázmány Péter Catholic University.

Today the square is known mainly for its terraces. The district council describes it as one of Józsefváros’s most popular hospitality and pedestrian spaces, and in 2024, after a hotel opened at number 3, it redrew the division of the terrace areas among the venues. In the 1990s the square and its surroundings were a nightlife area; We Love Budapest names Tilos az Á and, a little lower down in Krúdy utca, the Darshan Udvar.

It fits well with a walk through the Palace Quarter, whose former aristocratic residences, atmospheric squares and nearby National Museum and Szabó Ervin Library give the district its character. Local notices sometimes announce temporary closures around the square, so check jozsefvaros.hu if you are planning a visit.
tips: Terraces are the draw, so choose a spot on the square itself and expect the area to be busy in warm weather. Check venue pages for what is on offer rather than assuming.
Look for the Mikszáth statue in its corner and the plaques on the house fronts; the plaque for Irinyi marks the site of one of his workshops.
The Hungarian National Museum and the Szabó Ervin Library are close by, so the square works as a break between two cultural stops.
Residents live all around the square, so keep noise down in the evening. The district council’s website announces temporary works or event closures affecting the square.

history.intro: The square’s history is tied to two writers and to one house. Sources agree on the main outline but differ on the exact year of the second renaming.

sections.heading: From Reviczky tér to Mikszáth tér
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia says the square had no name in the nineteenth century. In 1900 it was named Reviczky tér, after the poet Gyula Reviczky, who had died the year before. It was renamed after Mikszáth following his death: the Wikipedia article says 1911, while We Love Budapest says the square was renamed when he died in 1910, so the sources differ by a year. Reviczky’s name passed to a neighbouring street. Mikszáth lived at number 1 in his last years.

sections.heading: The house at number 1
paragraphs: We Love Budapest says Irinyi’s match factory worked on the site of number 1 from 1839 until 1869, while Hungarian Wikipedia calls it one of his Pest workshops. Later the building was a school: the Sacré Coeur Sophianum girls’ school was here until 1948, and a Piarist gymnasium from 1953 to 2011. The humanities faculty of Pázmány Péter Catholic University has been there since.

sections.heading: Statues, nightlife and terraces
paragraphs: According to We Love Budapest, a statue of a reading girl by Ferenc Kovács stood on the square from 1954 until 1960, when it was moved to Tomori köz in the thirteenth district; the Mikszáth statue, made for the fiftieth anniversary of his death, followed. The 1990s brought a nightlife scene, and later the terraces, whose layout the district council revised in 2024 and set into its public-space rules in February 2025.

name: Zsámbék Church Ruins
intro: The ruined Premonstratensian church at Zsámbék, in Pest County west of Budapest, is a three-aisled basilica in late Romanesque and early Gothic style, built around 1220. Part of its vault fell in the earthquake of 1763 and the church has stood as a ruin since; it is now a protected monument, its two towers and stone arches still showing the scale of the original.
about: The Zsámbék Romtemplom is what remains of a thirteenth-century Premonstratensian church and monastery. Hungarian Wikipedia describes a three-aisled basilica with three apses and two towers but no transept. The south-eastern tower still has its original stone spire, while the north-western one is much lower and has a sheet-metal roof.

The site includes the stone collection, the Kőtár, housed in the former monastery ruins beside the church. Among the surviving monastery remains Hungarian Wikipedia lists a barrel-vaulted hall, the former refectory, the foundation of the cloister and a cellar system. Access and works change, so check the town’s page before you go.

The heritage register’s photo caption calls it one of the most romantic places in Hungary and notes that it often hosts weddings and outdoor events. News reports of a debate about how to protect the ruin add that some experts argue it is built of soft sandstone that keeps deteriorating.

Zsámbék lies in the Budakeszi district of Pest County, and Hungarian Wikipedia places it 35 kilometres west of Budapest, at the foot of Nyakas hill. The town also has a baroque castle of the Zichy family, so the ruin can be combined with a walk in the old centre. Plan the journey with the getting-around guide, since this is a day trip.
A redevelopment competition for the site was launched in 2023, and the plans have been debated since. Check the town’s official website for the current state of access and works before you travel.
tips: Check the town of Zsámbék’s official website, and the ruin’s own page, for current access, any works on the site and event days before you set out; redevelopment plans have been under discussion since 2023.
The Kőtár stone collection beside the church is part of the site, so ask on arrival where it can be seen. Wear sturdy shoes, since the ground in and around a ruin is uneven.
The ruin is a protected monument and also used for events, so treat the walls and stones with care and do not climb on them.

The two towers of unequal height are the ruin’s most recognisable feature and are worth photographing from a distance. The town’s website lists other sights in Zsámbék that can be combined with the visit.

history.intro: The church combines royal patronage, Ottoman-era upheaval and a nineteenth-century decision to preserve a ruin as a ruin. Dates below come from the town’s website and Hungarian Wikipedia.

sections.heading: A knight’s foundation and the Premonstratensians
paragraphs: The town’s website ties the basilica to Aynard, a knight who came to Hungary in the queen’s retinue and was given Zsámbék by King Béla III; his descendants built the church around 1220. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that it was already standing before 1235 and was dedicated to St John the Baptist. A Premonstratensian community lived in the neighbouring monastery, and Béla IV confirmed the church’s donation charter in 1258.

Hungarian Wikipedia reports that King Matthias gave the monastery to the Pauline order in 1475. After Buda fell to the Ottomans in 1541 the monastery became a fortress, and the Zichy family acquired Zsámbék in 1689.

sections.heading: The earthquake of 1763
paragraphs: An earthquake on 28 June 1763 brought down the vault and side wall of the north aisle. The church was left without an owner, local people carried off stones, and the villagers built a new church in the town centre.

sections.heading: Saving the ruin
paragraphs: In the 1870s the historians Flóris Rómer and Imre Henszlmann urged that the building be saved, and in 1889 the minister Ágoston Trefort commissioned the architect István Möller. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, Möller’s work between 1896 and 1900 secured only what was structurally necessary and left the ruin as a ruin. In 1934 Kálmán Lux uncovered the monastery walls on the north side. In 2023 the town launched a design competition for the site, and the plans have been debated since.
